procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated 14th May 1963 of the Calcutta High Court in Appeal from Order No. 44 of 1958.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings:
1. A single judge of the Calcutta High Court dismissed the appellant's petition under Article 226 on 11-9-1957 on the grounds of inordinate delay and failure to raise the jurisdictional objection during departmental proceedings.
2. A Division Bench of the Calcutta High Court dismissed the appeal from the single judge's decision, primarily on the ground of inordinate delay, although they were inclined to believe that the rules of natural justice had been violated during the departmental inquiry. The Division Bench also rejected the appellant's explanation for the delay.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court by certificate under Article 133 of the Constitution of India.

directions: The parties will bear their own costs.

issue.issue_text: Whether a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution is liable to be dismissed on the ground of laches or inordinate delay.

law.point: The power to grant relief under Article 226 of the Constitution is a discretionary power.
law.text: It has been made clear more than once that the power to give relief under Article 226 is a discretionary power. This is specially true in the case of power to issue writs in the nature of mandamus.

law.point: Delay is a key factor that High Courts consider when exercising their discretion under Article 226.
law.text: Among the several matters which the Hi.gh Courts rightly take into consideration in the exercise of that discretion is the delay made bv the aj!'grieved party in seekinj!' this special remedy and what excuse there is for it.

law.point: A petitioner seeking the extraordinary remedy of a writ must approach the court at the earliest reasonably possible opportunity.
law.text: In such cases, it is imperative, if the petitioner wants to invoke the extraordinary remedies available under Article 226 of the Constitu•ion, that he should come to Court at the earliest reasonably possible ooportunity.

law.point: The rule that delay can defeat a writ petition is not nullified simply because a civil suit on the same matter would still be within the limitation period.
law.text: we do not think that the rule that delay defeats the rights of a party to seek redress, by means of prerogative Writ under Article 226 of the Constitution, could be held to be abrogated merely because, if the claim had been brought in a Civil Court, the period of limitation would not have expired.

law.point: The limitation period for a civil suit can be used as a reasonable standard to measure delay, and a delay longer than that period will almost always be considered unreasonable.
law.text: It appears to us however that the maximum period fixed by the legislature as the time within which the relief by a suit in a civil Court must be brought may ordinarily be taken to be a reasonable standard by which delay in seeking remedy under Article 226 can be measured... but where the delay is more than this period, it will almost always be proper for the Court to hold that it is unreasonable".

application.point: The Supreme Court affirmed the High Court's decision to dismiss the appellant's petition on the ground of delay.
application.text: The ,High Court w .. right in dismiasing the appellant's petition 012 the ground of delay.

application.point: The Court refused to interfere with the discretion exercised by the High Court in dismissing the petition for delay.
application.text: At any rate, we do r.ot think that the discretion of the learned Single Judge and the Division Bench, with regard to a delay which defeated the petitioner's right to a discretionary relief, could be interfered with by us in this case.

application.point: The Court noted that if there is significant delay, a suit for damages may be a more appropriate remedy than a writ petition.
application.text: If there is delay in getting an adiudication, .a suit for damages actually sustained by wrongful dismissal may become the more or even the only appropriate means of redress.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that a writ petition under Article 226 can be dismissed on the ground of laches or inordinate delay. The Court reasoned that relief under Article 226 is an extraordinary and discretionary remedy, not an absolute right. A petitioner must approach the court promptly. The fact that a regular civil suit might still be within the limitation period does not prevent the court from dismissing a writ petition for delay. The Court upheld the High Court's exercise of its discretion to dismiss the petition on this ground.

issue.issue_text: Whether disputed questions of fact, such as allegations of bias, mala fides, or lack of due opportunity in departmental proceedings, can be decided in a writ petition under Article 226.

facts: The petitioner filed a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution.

In the petition, the petitioner raised several allegations against the departmental proceedings, including claims of bias, ill-will, mala fides, and denial of a due opportunity to be heard and produce evidence.
These allegations were contested by the state, with both sides making conflicting assertions in their affidavits.
law: The Supreme Court reiterated the established legal principle that proceedings under Article 226 (writ petitions) are generally not the appropriate forum for deciding seriously disputed questions of fact.
The power to grant relief under Article 226 is discretionary.
The Court cited its previous ruling in *Union of India v. T. R. Varma* to support the practice of not deciding such factual disputes in writ proceedings.
application: The Court identified that the petitioner's allegations of bias, mala fides, and lack of a fair hearing were "so largely questions of fact."
It found that it would be difficult to decide these issues based merely on the "conflicting assertions made by affidavits" from the two parties.
The Court distinguished this type of case, which involves contested facts, from a case where a tax is imposed under a clearly void law.
It determined that a more just and proper decision on such factual questions could be reached in other proceedings, specifically an ordinary civil suit.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that disputed questions of fact, such as allegations of bias or mala fides in departmental proceedings, cannot be decided in a writ petition under Article 226. The Court reasoned that such matters are difficult to resolve based solely on conflicting affidavits and that the proper remedy for the aggrieved party is to file a suit in a civil court, which is better equipped to handle such factual disputes.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution is liable to be dismissed on the ground of laches or inordinate delay.
appellant_arguments: The application under Article 226 was made within a period of 3 years from the original order of dismissal, which would have been within the time limit for a civil suit seeking a declaration that the dismissal was wrongful.
respondent_arguments: There was an inordinate delay on the part of the appellant in approaching the High Court, which justifies the dismissal of the petition.

arguments.issue_text: Whether disputed questions of fact, such as allegations of bias, mala fides, or lack of due opportunity in departmental proceedings, can be decided in a writ petition under Article 226.
appellant_arguments: The appellant was denied due opportunity to adduce relevant evidence or cross-examine witnesses.
The Deputy Commissioner of Police who passed the dismissal order was in the position of a complainant and could not act as a judge in the matter.
The order of dismissal was vitiated by actual bias and mala fides on the part of the dismissing authority.
respondent_arguments: These are seriously disputed questions of fact, with both sides making conflicting assertions in affidavits, and therefore cannot be decided in a writ petition.

cases.case_name: State of Madhya Pradesh v. Bhailal & Ors.
cases.principle: The maximum period fixed by the legislature for a civil suit can ordinarily be taken as a reasonable standard to measure delay in seeking a remedy under Article 226. The court retains discretion to refuse the extraordinary remedy under Article 226 and leave the party to their ordinary remedy in a civil court.

cases.case_name: Union of India v. T. R. Varma
cases.principle: It is not the practice of Courts to decide disputed questions of fact in proceedings under Article 226 of the Constitution.

cases.case_name: Rabindra Nath Bose & Ors. v. Union of India & Ors.
cases.principle: A person who seeks to invoke the extraordinary remedies available under the Constitution should approach the Court at the earliest reasonably possible opportunity.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The rule that unreasonable delay defeats the right of a party to seek redress through a prerogative writ under Article 226 of the Constitution is not abrogated merely because a civil suit for the same claim would be within the statutory period of limitation. A petitioner seeking to invoke the extraordinary remedies under Article 226 must approach the court at the earliest reasonably possible opportunity.
obiter: The maximum period fixed by the legislature as the time within which relief by a suit in a civil court must be brought may ordinarily be taken to be a reasonable standard by which delay in seeking remedy under Article 226 can be measured.
No relief should be given to petitioners who, without any reasonable explanation, approach the Court under Article 32 of the Constitution after inordinate delay.
The special remedy provided in Article 226 is not intended to supersede completely the modes of obtaining relief by an action in a civil court.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Court refused to exercise its discretion to interfere with the order of dismissal, finding that the appellant's inordinate and unexplained delay in approaching the court was a sufficient ground for dismissal of the writ petition. The extraordinary remedy under Article 226 is not meant for stale demands, and the appellant's failure to act promptly justified the High Court's decision.
legal_tests_applied: The exercise of jurisdiction under Article 226 is discretionary, and relief can be refused on the ground of laches or inordinate delay.
If there has been unreasonable delay, the court ought not ordinarily to lend its aid to a party by the extraordinary remedy of mandamus.
Where a prima facie triable issue is raised regarding the merits of a claim, the court should ordinarily refuse to issue a writ and leave the party to seek remedy in a civil court.
The time limit for a civil suit is not a rule of limitation for a writ petition; the court can refuse relief even if a suit would have been within time, based on the principle of laches.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant was guilty of inordinate delay in filing the writ petition, and the explanation provided for this delay was disbelieved by the lower courts on good and reasonable grounds.

The argument that the petition was filed within the limitation period for a civil suit was rejected, as the discretionary writ jurisdiction is not bound by such limitation periods and can be refused on grounds of laches.

The appellant's claims of bias, mala fides, and lack of due opportunity were disputed questions of fact, which are not suitable for determination in a writ petition and are better left for a civil suit.
It is imperative for a petitioner seeking the extraordinary remedy under Article 226 to approach the court at the earliest reasonably possible time, which the appellant failed to do.
why_respondent_won: The respondent successfully argued that the appellant's petition should be dismissed due to inordinate delay, as laches is a well-established ground for a court to refuse to exercise its discretionary writ jurisdiction.

The respondent successfully contended that the appellant's allegations of bias and mala fides constituted seriously disputed questions of fact, which are inappropriate for resolution in summary proceedings under Article 226.
policy_considerations: In cases involving public servants seeking reinstatement, promptness is essential so that the State is not called upon to pay unnecessarily for a period when the servant was not employed.
Delay may make the motives of a dismissed servant, who may have a technical ground to urge against the dismissal, suspect.
It could not have been the intention of the Constitution makers that the High Court or Supreme Court should go into stale demands after a lapse of years.
Interfering in such delayed cases would only prolong litigation, as the court could only quash the dismissal and allow new proceedings, giving the appellant another long period to contest the matter.
